common_name: Apple Blossom Amaryllis (Soft Pink-and-White Bicolor Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Apple Blossom is one of the best-selling amaryllis cultivars, bearing soft pink-and-white bicolor flowers, and naturalizes in the ground as a permanent perennial in zone 8-10 gardens.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Apple Blossom is one of the most widely sold amaryllis cultivars, prized for large, softly blushed pink-and-white bicolor blooms that read as delicate and romantic compared with the bolder solid reds and whites of many other cultivars, produced on tall, sturdy stalks in spring. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, where it naturalizes and multiplies over the years into an increasingly impressive clump. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after bloom rather than cutting it early, since the leaves recharge the bulb for next year's flowers, and it can also be forced into bloom indoors as a classic holiday container amaryllis by planting with about a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Minerva is one of the most popular and widely available amaryllis cultivars, bearing bold red flowers with a crisp white star pattern at the center.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Minerva bears large, vivid red flowers with a distinctive crisp white star radiating from the center of each bloom, making it one of the most recognizable and widely sold amaryllis cultivars, striking both in the garden and as a classic holiday container bulb. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, naturalizing and multiplying into an increasingly full clump over the years. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering rather than cutting it early, since the leaves recharge the bulb, and for container forcing plant with roughly a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix for traditional winter bloom indoors.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost in warm, fertile, moist soil in full sun; Durban is grown primarily for its vividly striped pink, orange, and bronze foliage, among the most colorful ornamental-leaf cannas in the trade.

directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in warm, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun. Durban is grown chiefly for its dramatic foliage, with broad leaves striped in shifting bands of hot pink, orange, and bronze that provide season-long color even between the plant's orange flower spikes, making it one of the showiest foliage cannas available for tropical-look Gulf South landscaping and large container plantings. Like other cannas it thrives with generous water and rich soil, tolerating even boggy conditions at a pond edge. In zones below its hardiness range, dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter after the first frost blackens the foliage; in zone 8-10 gardens it can typically be left in the ground with a heavy mulch layer for winter protection.

common_name: President Canna (Classic Heirloom Solid Scarlet-Red Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost in warm, fertile, moist soil in full sun; President is a classic, widely planted heirloom canna with plain green leaves and large, bold scarlet-red flowers, historically one of the most common garden cannas.

directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in warm, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun. President is a long-cultivated heirloom canna bearing broad, solid green leaves and large, brilliant scarlet-red flowers on sturdy, compact stalks, representing the classic, unfussy garden canna look that anchored countless Southern flower beds for generations before the modern trend toward colorful striped and bronze-leaved cultivars. Its reliable, heavy bloom and tough constitution have kept it in continuous cultivation despite flashier newer introductions. Like other cannas it thrives with generous water and rich soil. In zones below its hardiness range, dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter after the first frost blackens the foliage; in zone 8-10 gardens it can typically be left in the ground with a heavy mulch layer for winter protection.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost in warm, fertile, moist soil in full sun; Cleopatra is a genetically unstable novelty canna that produces an unpredictable mix of solid green and maroon leaves, and yellow, red, and mixed-color flowers, sometimes all on the same plant.

directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in warm, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun. Cleopatra is a genuinely unusual novelty canna known for genetic instability that causes individual leaves to emerge solid green or solid maroon in unpredictable patches on the same plant, paired with flowers that can be solid yellow, solid red, or streaked and spotted with both colors, sometimes even on the same flower stalk, making every plant a bit of a surprise from season to season. This chimeric, ever-changing display has made it a favorite conversation piece among collectors and canna enthusiasts despite, or because of, its unpredictability. Like other cannas it thrives with generous water and rich soil, tolerating boggy conditions at a pond edge. In zones below its hardiness range, dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter; in zone 8-10 gardens it can typically be left in the ground with heavy winter mulch.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost in warm, fertile, moist soil in full sun; Stuttgart is grown primarily as a dramatic foliage accent, with large leaves heavily marbled and streaked in white over gray-green, needing a bit more shade protection than green-leaved cannas to avoid leaf scorch.

directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in warm, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, since the heavily variegated white-and-gray leaves can scorch in the most intense sun and heat. Stuttgart is grown chiefly as a bold foliage accent, with large leaves dramatically marbled and streaked in white over a soft gray-green base, giving it a ghostly, eye-catching presence that stands apart from typical solid-green or brightly striped canna foliage; its small orange flowers are secondary to the striking leaves. Like other cannas it thrives with generous water and rich soil, tolerating even boggy ground at a pond edge. In zones below its hardiness range, dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter after the first frost blackens the foliage; in zone 8-10 gardens it can typically be left in the ground with a heavy mulch layer for winter protection.
